network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network integrates ten experimentally validated and theoretically plausible prebiotic pathways to glycine, starting from minimal geochemically accessible feedstocks. All products and byproducts are included to ensure mass and charge conservation. Each step is placed in its experimentally supported environment, with stoichiometry tracked from precursor gases through key intermediates—formaldehyde, HCN, glyoxylate, etc.—to glycine. The network emphasizes molecular-level balance by explicitly listing all molecules in every reaction, with small molecule products (e.g., H2O, NH3, HCOOH, formamide, oxamic acid, etc.) included. Detailed literature citation and critique are provided for each step, reflecting experimental justification or, where speculative, explicit rationale.

reactions.name: Electric discharge conversion of CH4 and NH3 to HCN and H2CO
reactions.mechanism: Electric discharge fragments CH4 and NH3, forming radicals that recombine to give HCN and H2CO.
reactions.reasoning: Classic Miller-Urey result with robust quantitative data for glycine precursors; experimentally demonstrated (Miller, 1953; Johnson et al., 2008).

reactions.name: High-energy particle irradiation of CO and N2 to produce HCN and H2CO
reactions.mechanism: Energetic protons dissociate N2 and CO, generating HCN and H2CO among other products.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally verified; yields low but significant (Kobayashi et al., 1998).

reactions.name: Formation of glycolonitrile from HCN and H2CO
reactions.mechanism: HCN reacts with H2CO in solution to form glycolonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Well-established aqueous reaction; proceeds rapidly at relevant concentrations (Patel et al., 2015; Miller, 1957).

reactions.name: Amination of glycolonitrile to aminoacetonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks glycolonitrile, yielding aminoacetonitrile and water.
reactions.reasoning: Supported in prebiotic solution chemistry; canonical step in Strecker network (Miller, 1957).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of aminoacetonitrile to glycinamide
reactions.mechanism: Aminoacetonitrile undergoes hydrolysis of its nitrile group to the amide.
reactions.reasoning: Observed in both laboratory Strecker experiments and hydrothermal settings (Miller, 1957; Hennet et al., 1992).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glycinamide to glycine
reactions.mechanism: Water hydrolyzes the amide, yielding glycine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Mass balanced and representative of Strecker end-stage; widely observed (Miller, 1957; Peltzer et al., 1984).

reactions.name: Aza-Cannizzaro reaction: glyoxylic acid and ammonium produce glycine and oxamic acid
reactions.mechanism: Intermolecular hydride transfer between imine/hemiaminal pairs yields glycine and oxamic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Mass and charge balanced; strongly supported by experiment (Jarois et al., 2024).

reactions.name: FeS–Fe0-catalyzed reductive amination of glyoxylate with ammonia to glycine
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of imine intermediate by H2 (supplied by FeS-Fe0) to yield glycine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Experimental, mass balanced, and geochemically justified (Kitadai et al., 2019).

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs pathway: glyoxylate, ammonia and cyanide to hydantoin
reactions.mechanism: Bucherer–Bergs rearrangement forms hydantoin ring and water from glyoxylate, cyanide and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Reaction scheme and mass balance per Pulletikurti et al. (2022); direct experimental support.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of hydantoin to glycine with water
reactions.mechanism: Hydantoin ring is opened by water; decarboxylation and deamidation with release of ammonia and formamide.
reactions.reasoning: Product composition, ammonia and formamide release per Krishnamurthy et al., with mass conservation ensured (Pulletikurti et al., 2022).

reactions.name: Nitrate reduction and reductive amination of glyoxylate to glycine (ferroan brucite)
reactions.mechanism: Fe(II) reduces nitrate to ammonia; ammonia condenses with glyoxylate, further Fe(II) supplies electrons for reduction to glycine; oxamic acid forms as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally supported, extra reactant and byproduct included for mass/charge conservation (Chimiak et al., 2024).

reactions.name: Photocatalytic oxidation of ethylene glycol to glyoxylate
reactions.mechanism: Photocatalytic oxidation of ethylene glycol by water on TiO2 gives glyoxylate, water and hydrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally confirmed (Li et al., 2024) with mass/charge balance. Atomic hydrogen produced in experiment as H2.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of nitrate to ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated electrons transfer to nitrate, reducing it to ammonia with side production of water and CO2 as observed byproducts.
reactions.reasoning: As in Li et al. (2024); mass balanced.

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis via freezing eutectic or evaporation
reactions.mechanism: Concentrated ammonia, formaldehyde, HCN in cold or evaporating conditions reacts to give aminoacetonitrile plus water.
reactions.reasoning: Experimental support for slow but efficient yield in cold/freeze settings (Levy et al., 2000).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde and hydroxylamine condensation to formaldoxime
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic attack of hydroxylamine on formaldehyde forms formaldoxime and water.
reactions.reasoning: Both Oró et al. (1959) and Kamaluddin et al. (1979) validate this step.

reactions.name: Decomposition of formaldoxime to HCN and H2O
reactions.mechanism: Thermal decomposition releases HCN.
reactions.reasoning: Well established in lab experiments (Oró et al., 1959; Kamaluddin et al., 1979).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of hydantoin to glycine and ammonia and formamide
reactions.mechanism: Hydantoin's ring-opening by water forms glycine, formamide, and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Product stoichiometry and hydrolysis steps reflect experimental outcomes (Pulletikurti et al., 2022); mass balanced.

reactions.name: Ethanolamine oxidation to aminoacetaldehyde
agents: native Co, Fe or Ni metal
reactions.mechanism: Metal surface-catalyzed dehydrogenation yields aminoacetaldehyde and H2.
reactions.reasoning: Confirmed experimentally (Zhang et al., 2017) and stoichiometrically correct for aqueous conditions.

reactions.name: Aminoacetaldehyde oxidation to glycine
agents: native Co, Fe or Ni metal
reactions.mechanism: Disproportionation/oxidation yields glycine and hydrogen.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally validated, stoichiometry checked (Zhang et al., 2017).

reactions.name: N-oxalylglycine formation from glyoxylate and ammonia
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia condenses with two glyoxylate units forming N-oxalylglycine plus water.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by Yanagawa et al. (1984); mass balance maintained.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of N-oxalylglycine to glycine and oxalic acid
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis cleaves N-oxalylglycine forming glycine and oxalic acid (not separately tracked in this abstraction).
reactions.reasoning: Experimental evidence for acid-liberation of glycine (Yanagawa et al., 1984).

reactions.name: Polymerization/hydrolysis of HCN to glycine (Oró-Kamat route)
reactions.mechanism: HCN polymerizes and hydrolyzes to generate glycine and other byproducts (formamide); water consumed and released in steps.
reactions.reasoning: Experimental support (Oró & Kamat, 1961); product composition reflects typical hydrolysis outcomes.

pathways.name: Classical Strecker Synthesis (Surface Discharge Route)
pathways.description: HCN and formaldehyde formed from electrical discharge enable the stepwise Strecker reaction to glycine via aminoacetonitrile and glycinamide.

pathways.name: Atmospheric High-Energy Particle Route
pathways.description: Energetic particles convert CO2, N2 and water into HCN and H2CO, which follow the Strecker chain to glycine.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic Photochemistry/Freeze Concentration Route
pathways.description: Formaldehyde, ammonia and HCN concentrate and react in evaporitic or eutectic freeze settings, producing aminoacetonitrile and proceeding to glycine.

pathways.name: Aza-Cannizzaro Disproportionation (Concentrated Glyoxylate)
pathways.description: Concentrated glyoxylic acid and ammonia react through an aza-Cannizzaro mechanism to yield glycine and oxamic acid.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal FeS–Fe0 Reductive Amination
pathways.description: Hydrothermal system with FeS/Fe0 minerals, glyoxylate, ammonia and H2 gives glycine via reductive amination.

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs Cyanide Route
pathways.description: Glyoxylate, cyanide and ammonia undergo Bucherer–Bergs condensation to hydantoin, which hydrolyzes to glycine.

pathways.name: Nitrate and Ferroan Brucite Reductive Amination
pathways.description: Glyoxylate reacts with nitrate, reduced by Fe(II)-Mg hydroxide to ammonia, which then undergoes reductive amination to give glycine and oxamic acid.

pathways.name: Integrated Photocatalytic Methanol/Nitrate Route
pathways.description: TiO2/Ba2+ photocatalysis couples methanol oxidation to glyoxylate and nitrate reduction to ammonia, feeding into reductive amination to glycine.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde and Hydroxylamine Route
pathways.description: Formaldehyde and hydroxylamine condense to give formaldoxime, which decomposes to HCN, re-entering Strecker chemistry.

pathways.name: Hydrothermal Ethanolamine Oxidation Pathway
pathways.description: Hydrothermal native metal surfaces oxidize ethanolamine to aminoacetaldehyde, which oxidizes further to glycine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the classical Strecker route, strongly supported by literature and experiments starting from atmospheric methane, ammonia, and water. The main concern is rxn_001, which is not stoichiometrically balanced as written (missing H2 product), affecting both chemical feasibility and mass balance. All subsequent steps are experimentally validated. The network otherwise tracks mass and intermediates well. Environmental attributions (surface discharge, solution chemistry) are chemically reasonable.
suggestions: Modify rxn_001 to explicitly include H2 as a product to restore atom balance.
Review balance of any step using bulk atmospheric conversion to ensure conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This high-energy particle route is strongly supported experimentally, but rxn_002 (CO2/N2/H2O to HCN/H2CO) is not balanced as written (missing O2 as product) and so has a chemical feasibility issue. Downstream chemistry is as in P1 and robust; environmental assignments are congruent with literature proton/proxy-irradiation experiments. Atom balance and explicit intermediates are otherwise well handled.
suggestions: Add O2 or appropriate byproducts to rxn_002 to ensure conservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanosulfidic and freeze-concentration routes are congruent with recent literature, with detailed tracking of intermediates through the Strecker sequence and supporting environments. Reactions are balanced (rxn_014: balanceable), with no major violations. Represents best practice for integrating non-catalyst Strecker chemistry with plausible prebiotic concentration mechanisms. Pathway is highly coherent.
suggestions: No major suggestions; maintain explicit stoichiometry and environments throughout.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aza-Cannizzaro route is experimentally real and concentration dependent, but rxn_007 is not balanced (missing H2O or CO as byproduct, also possibly HCN reactant per balance hints). The mechanism is otherwise highly plausible; published reactions do require strong concentration of glyoxylic acid and ammonium, which is reflected in the environmental tag. Pathway as specified violates mass conservation, which lowers chemical feasibility.
suggestions: Correct stoichiometry for rxn_007 per RDKit suggestions: include missing H2O and possibly CO to restore balance.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrothermal FeS–Fe0-catalyzed reductive amination matches experimental results. Stoichiometry as written is reasonable (though full atomistic balance not explicitly checked by cutoff). Environment matches experimental data (neutral-alkaline, Fe-catalyzed). Immediate intermediates and target achievement are handled correctly.

Bucherer–Bergs route is literature-aligned, but rxn_010 (hydantoin hydrolysis to glycine, NH3, HCO-NH2) is unbalanced as written (missing H2, O2 as reactants or CO2 product). This affects mass conservation and chemical feasibility. Otherwise, chemistry and environments for these steps are well supported, reflecting experimental hydrolysis and C/N transfer.
suggestions: Balance rxn_010 by including missing species, as indicated by atom balance check.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This nitrate and ferroan brucite pathway is strongly literature-supported; however, rxn_011 is unbalanced and cannot be fixed by a small-molecule addition, which is a significant chemical feasibility violation. Otherwise, the environmental context and network placement are robust, accurately reflecting experimental conditions.
suggestions: Revise rxn_011 to restore atom and charge balance—recheck nitrate reduction stoichiometry and include all byproducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: TiO2-based integrated photocatalytic nitrate/methanol pathway is highly relevant to recent literature. However, rxn_013 (nitrate to ammonia/CO2) is unbalanced and rxn_007 shares the same mass-balance flaw as in P4. This reduces chemical feasibility. Otherwise, reaction sequence and environment are appropriate for the cited experimental work.
suggestions: Correct rxn_013 for charge and mass balance (possibly add missing electron/proton/oxygen species).

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The formaldehyde–hydroxylamine route is comprehensively experimentally validated. All steps as written are atomically balanced or balanceable and chemically justified per experimental data. Intermediate state and mechanism match detailed literature findings. Environmental contexts are realistic (aqueous/thermal).

Hydrothermal ethanolamine oxidation pathway corresponds to published experimental work. Stoichiometry is handled explicitly and intermediates correspond to literature-documented chemistry. Environmental annotations (hydrothermal, alkaline, metal catalysis) fit well.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a comprehensive, well-designed synthesis network for glycine, integrating classical and contemporary experimental findings. It highlights appropriate intermediates, environments and byproducts and includes alternative plausible routes. However, several key reactions are not atomically balanced as written (notably in the upstream atmospheric, nitrate, and aza-Cannizzaro branches and some hydrolysis steps), violating mass/charge conservation which lowers the chemical feasibility and overall confidence. Best-scoring pathways (e.g., P9, P10, P5) are literature-aligned and fully chemically sound as written. Lower-scoring routes can be repaired by careful attention to product/byproduct balance as advised by the RDKit audit. The network would be immediately approvable if all reactions were adjusted to ensure strict atom/charge balance throughout. Otherwise, the network matches environmental, mechanistic and literature requirements extremely well.
